text: Based on the LCA/TEA inputs, the model provides results for optimized biorefinery location, movement of feedstock, and total carbon abated. The locations that BILT considers for facility siting are provided via an OR-SAGE framework. OR-SAGE considers several constraints to determine regions of feasibility for siting. For this analysis, BILT was run using a 50-mile plant spacing for the baseline results. For comparison, the model was also run using a 75-mile spacing as a sensitivity analysis. This parameter applies to facilities that could be built in the future. Some of the analyses used existing 33 facilities. The facilities that process the soybeans into soybean oil already exist, and data about them were gathered from the National Oilseed Processors Association website (NOPA, 2025). The bio-oil generated via the CFP pathway and biocrude from the HTL pathway were assumed to be transported to and hydrotreated at existing petroleum refineries. The locations for existing petroleum refineries were retrieved from the Energy Information Administration’s U.S. Energy Atlas (2024). The analysis was run with a minimum facility usage factor of 0.9, meaning that a facility would have to process at least 90% of its nameplate feedstock processing capacity to be sited. This is a strict utilization requirement. Realistically, a refinery would run approximately 330 days a year (Kinchin, 2020) and will strive to maintain 60% of its nameplate capacity. The analysis does not account for existing facilities, other than the existing petroleum facilities and soybean processing facilities already noted. This removes the complication of interacting with the existing use of facilities. The main output of a BILT analysis is a carbon avoidance cost curve. The results that are discussed in this section are primarily from the 90% of maximum CO stage. 2 Moving from avoiding 90% to avoiding 100% of the maximum carbon avoidance level results in a large increase in the number of facilities that are constructed. This is expected since the model needs to utilize 100% of the feedstocks and it achieves carbon minimization by minimizing emissions from transporting biomass. This leads to a significantly larger number of facilities to reduce the distance the biomass is moved. The biomass available for producing biofuels in this study is displayed in Figure 5-1. BT23 data is provided at a county level, and a county’s color indicates the amount of biomass per unit area. For corn stover and pine, availability was limited to the amount produced when a price of $80/ton is offered to the growers. 34 Figure 5-1 Availability of Biomass Derived from the Billion-Ton 2023 Study (DOE, 2024), Shaded by Biomass Density 35 BILT was used to analyze 11 biofuel pathways. These pathways differed in the feedstocks they used, the conversion processes employed, and the products that were generated. A listing of the pathways is provided in Appendix D. 5.1.1 BILT Siting Decisions The BILT analysis focused on a scenario with minimum facility spacing of 50 miles (facilities are spaced further apart when feedstocks are gathered over a larger area).
